relations.myth: Social and ritual contrast between Dantò and Freda
relations.note: Dantò’s protective working motherhood contrasts with Freda’s luxury and frustrated romance.
They fight over a male spirit; varying versions explain Dantò’s wounds or Freda’s pierced heart.

relations.myth: Dantò and Freda contend over Ogou
relations.note: Dantò is Ogou’s lover or partner; traditions variously specify Feray, Badagri, Chango, or another Ogou.
Some oral genealogies identify Ti Jean as Dantò’s son or the child she carries.
A documented praise-song calls Dantò Ti Jean’s woman; some traditions call him her husband or lover.
Some houses treat Ti Jean as Dantò’s closely allied ritual companion.
Modern spirit lists distinguish Jean Petwo from Ti Jean and identify him as Dantò’s spouse or lover.
Some lineages name Anaïs as Dantò’s daughter and identify her as the child in Dantò’s icon.
Modern queer and diasporic accounts sometimes identify Simbi Makaya as Dantò’s husband or partner.
Some classifications identify Red-Eyes as Dantò’s enraged or hotter form; others consider her separate.
Where treated as a distinct lwa, Red-Eyes is classified as Dantò’s companion.
Lasirèn and Dantò are classified together as distinct female sacred possibilities within the Èzili complex.
Modern catalogues sometimes pair Marinette with Dantò in Petwo service, without recording a narrative encounter.

relations.myth: Later identification of Dantò at Bois Caïman
relations.note: Modern national tradition identifies Dantò with the power invoked at Bois Caïman, though early accounts do not.
Dantò is principally represented through the scarred dark Madonna and Child image associated with Częstochowa.
Some houses identify Dantò through Our Lady of Mount Carmel and observe her July feast.
Some houses use Our Lady of Prompt Succor as Dantò’s Catholic visual correspondence.
